turns.content: Hey sorry random question do I sort these binders by case year or dispute type A lot of folders are missing the year and some overlap topics so neither way is clean Also I keep replaying those phone transfers yesterday I feel like Gary is benching me from the front desk now Do you think that's what this is

I’d use **dispute type as the main binder grouping**, with a “Mixed/unclear” section for folders that don’t fit neatly. Within each group, sort by case year where it’s recorded and put “Year unknown” at the back—don’t guess missing dates. For overlapping topics, pick one primary category and add a cross-reference in the other. If there’s an existing office filing standard, follow that instead.

And those phone transfers clearly stuck with you, especially with the worry that you’re being moved away from the front desk. **The transfers alone don’t establish that Gary is benching you.** They could reflect coverage, routing, or a change in duties; you don’t yet know which.

My recommendation: use the filing system above, and ask Gary directly but neutrally: “After yesterday’s phone transfers, I wanted to check—should I still be covering the front desk as usual, or has the plan changed?” That gets you useful information without treating your worry as a settled fact.

I'll try the dispute type sort with a mixed section That's practical thanks

But about Gary I don't know if I can just ask him straight up like that without sounding paranoid What if he wasn't even thinking about the phones and now I've made it a thing

That makes sense—you want clarity without turning yesterday’s transfers into an issue Gary may not have been thinking about. You don’t have to mention the transfers or your worry to check what you should be doing.

Keep it routine and focused on today:
> “Once I finish these binders, should I cover the front desk or keep going with the filing?”

That’s a work-priority question, not an accusation. His answer can clarify today’s assignment, though it won’t necessarily tell you whether your role is changing longer-term.

The transfers alone still don’t establish that he’s benching you. My recommendation is to ask the routine priority question when you’re ready for your next task, rather than raise the bigger concern before you have more information.

The routine question approach feels safer yeah I can do that

But what if he says keep filing and that means I really am off the phones permanently Two days of messing up transfers and now I'm the filing person

It sounds like you’re worried that two rough days have turned into a lasting judgment about what you can handle. **“Keep filing” would tell you today’s assignment—not, by itself, that you’re permanently off the phones.**

It’s possible Gary wants you focused on filing, or wants more transfer practice before you cover the desk again. You don’t yet know his reason. Even if the mistakes prompted a temporary change, that wouldn’t automatically mean a permanent reassignment.

If he says “keep filing,” you can simply do that for now. At a calm moment, make a concrete request:
> “I’d like to get more confident with phone transfers. Could we run through the steps before I next cover the desk?”

My recommendation is to ask the routine priority question today and request a brief transfer refresher—not treat one assignment as a verdict on your role or ability.
Yeah but what if a refresher just reminds him I messed up and he keeps me off the phones longer

You’re worried that trying to fix the mistakes could draw more attention to them. That’s understandable when you’re already unsure where you stand.

**A refresher could bring the mistakes to mind, but there’s no evidence that asking for one would keep you off the phones longer.** I also can’t promise how Gary would respond. You don’t have to request it today just to settle the worry.

For now, ask the routine priority question and treat the answer as today’s assignment. Before you next handle calls, review any existing transfer instructions; if a step is still unclear, ask specifically: “Can you confirm how to transfer a call to ___?” That addresses a practical gap without turning it into a bigger discussion about your performance.

My recommendation is to clarify today’s work, then get whatever instruction you actually need before taking calls—not avoid useful help because of a reaction you can’t yet predict.
Right but what if I ask about covering the desk and he says keep filing and I just have to accept that

Yes—he might say “keep filing,” and if he’s assigning your work, you may need to follow that direction today. That’s the uncomfortable part: asking gives you information, but not control over his answer.

**Accepting today’s assignment isn’t accepting a permanent change to your role.** The transfers and a filing assignment still wouldn’t establish that he’s benching you.

You can say “Okay” without resolving everything on the spot. If you keep getting assigned filing instead of your usual desk work, it’s reasonable to ask:
> “I’ve been doing more filing lately. Is that temporary, or should I expect my usual duties to change?”

My recommendation is to follow today’s assignment and seek a clearer explanation if the change continues—not treat one “keep filing” as a final verdict.
